content: The guidelines should be adapted and implemented by developing or revising existing national policies, protocols, and guidelines in alignment with WHO recommendations. This process also involves creating tools to facilitate adaptation and implementation, as well as providing technical support to local implementers. This includes the development of training materials and quality indicators to ensure effective application. Barriers to the successful implementation and scaling up of these guidelines may arise from various factors. These include behaviors of women, parents, caregivers, families, or health workers, as well as issues related to the organization of care or health service delivery. For example, a mother attending a postnatal visit without her newborn or the lack of health information systems designed to document and monitor recommended practices, such as patient records and registers, can hinder progress. To address these barriers, a phased approach to adopting, adapting, and implementing the guideline recommendations is advisable. Strategies to overcome these challenges and facilitate implementation are detailed in Chapter 4 and Web Annex 5 of the guidelines. The impact of the guideline implementation will be monitored at health service, sub-national, and national levels using clearly defined criteria and indicators aligned with locally agreed targets. Data on the adoption of recommendations at country and regional levels will be collected and evaluated in collaboration with WHO monitoring and evaluation teams. This will be done in the short to medium term across WHO Member States through the SRMNCAH Policy Survey. A comprehensive monitoring framework will be developed once the guidelines are finalized. In the interim, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) has proposed indicators adapted from global recommendations. These include the average length of stay in health facilities after childbirth, disaggregated by mode of birth (vaginal or cesarean), and the percentage of women and newborns receiving postnatal care within two days of childbirth. Other indicators include the percentage of newborns receiving a hepatitis B birth dose vaccine within 24 hours of birth. Limitations of these indicators will be reviewed as the monitoring framework evolves. The Mother and Newborn Information for Tracking Outcomes and Results (MoNITOR) group will be consulted to identify recommended indicators for measuring postnatal care coverage and quality. These indicators will capture the core content of postnatal care contacts with women and newborns. The guidelines will be updated systematically and continuously to address evidence gaps identified during implementation. An Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) for maternal and newborn health recommendations will convene biannually to review WHO’s portfolio of recommendations, prioritize new and existing questions for development or updating, and address recommendations supported by low-certainty evidence. Recommendations will be regularly reviewed and updated as new evidence emerges. If no new evidence is identified, recommendations will be revalidated. Any concerns about the validity of recommendations will be promptly communicated via the guideline website, and updates will be made as necessary.
